p: From the first shot on Knoxlyn Ridge on the morning of July 1 to the last cavalry action east of town on the afternoon of July 3, the Battle of Gettysburg had consumed three days and approximately 51,000 men. Seven thousand were dead. The rest were wounded or missing. The fields and orchards and woodlots of Adams County, Pennsylvania — farmland, ordinary farmland — were covered with the wreckage of two armies.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 2 of 9

p: On July 4, while the town of Gettysburg tried to count its dead, the news arrived from the west: Vicksburg had fallen. Grant had split the Confederacy. Two disasters in two days.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 3 of 9

p: Lee began his retreat on July 4 in a driving rainstorm. Imboden's wagon train — seventeen miles of it, filled with wounded men who screamed with every jolt of the road — moved south and west toward Virginia. The army followed, battered, depleted, but intact. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. The opportunity to destroy Lee's army, if it existed, was not taken.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 4 of 9

p: The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years. There would be Cold Harbor and the Wilderness and Petersburg and the Shenandoah and Appomattox. But the moment when Confederate victory was possible — the moment when a successful invasion of the North might have forced a negotiated peace — had passed on the afternoon of July 3 at a stone wall in Pennsylvania.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 5 of 9

p: The copse of trees still stands. The stone wall has been rebuilt where it was torn apart in the fighting. A bronze marker — placed by veterans, not the government — stands near the spot where Armistead fell.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 6 of 9

p: It reads: 'The High Water Mark of the Rebellion.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 7 of 9

p: The ground is quiet now. The fields are green in summer, brown in fall, white in winter. The monuments stand in long rows along Seminary Ridge and Cemetery Ridge and the slopes of Culp's Hill and Little Round Top. There are 1,328 of them — more monuments per square mile than anywhere else on earth.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The High Water Mark”, paragraph 8 of 9

p: In July, when the heat is heavy and the air still, you can stand at The Angle and look west across the open fields and understand exactly what happened here, and why it mattered, and what it cost.
